title: Breadth-first search and shortest paths on an adjacency list

blocks.text: The page stores a graph as an **adjacency list**: each vertex keeps the set of its neighbours. Breadth-first search (BFS) from a vertex visits it, then all its neighbours, then theirs, using a queue and a *visited* set, and in an unweighted graph it finds a **shortest path**.

items: `new Graph<>(directed)`; `addEdge(from, to)` adds both vertices if new and the edge; in an undirected graph the edge goes both ways, in a directed one **only from `from` to `to`**. Neighbours are kept in the order their edges were added.
`bfs(start)` lists the vertices reached from `start` in BFS order, **each once**; an unknown `start` gives an empty list.
`shortestPath(from, to)` lists the vertices of a shortest path, both ends included; **no path (or an unknown vertex) gives an empty list**, and **a vertex's path to itself is just `[that vertex]`**.

blocks.text: Edges added (undirected): New York-Boston, New York-Philadelphia, Boston-Portland, Philadelphia-Washington.

cases.says: On the page's five-city map, bfs from New York and the shortest path from Portland to Washington match the page.
On a triangle, where two routes reach the same vertex, bfs lists every vertex exactly once.
In a directed graph an edge A to B is not an edge B to A, so neither bfs nor shortestPath walks it backwards.
Between two parts of a disconnected graph, or from or to a vertex the graph does not have, shortestPath is an empty list.
The shortest path from a vertex to itself is a list holding just that vertex.

concepts: Breadth-first search over an adjacency list, with a visited set, visits each vertex once and finds a shortest path in an unweighted graph.
In a directed graph an edge goes one way, while an undirected edge is stored in both vertices' neighbour sets.
